name: Amira Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get in at two, check the walk-in fridge, and write my prep list by hand on the back of yesterday's tickets. From five till eleven I run the grill at the Copper Pot, a busy brasserie on Mill Street, which on a Saturday means maybe ninety steaks and a lot of shouting. I love the moment when the whole line is in rhythm and nobody needs to speak. What wears me out is the heat, the burns on my forearms, and knowing the pay doesn't match how good we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone was scared of the robots and in the end it's a new till system and an app that writes the menu blurb. On the line I'd joke that the grill still needs a human who can smell when the fat's about to catch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't fix anything for me. My pay is still low, the rent on our flat above the bakery still goes up every spring, and I still have less than a month of money in the bank. AI being hype just means the old problems stay exactly where they were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, run the grill and train the new commis. I'd keep pushing the owner for a proper pay rise, because I've asked for a year and he keeps saying after Christmas. And I'd talk to the others about joining the hospitality union, because one person asking gets nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's a relief that nothing big is coming for my job, but the money worry sits in my stomach every month. One broken tooth or a burn that keeps me off work for two weeks and we're behind on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a burn could put you behind on rent. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter I caught my wrist on the salamander, the overhead grill, and needed four days off. No sick pay for the first three, so we ate pasta for a fortnight and Tomas, my partner, did extra night shifts on the buses. That's the real risk in my life, not a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a pay rise actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even fifty more a week would mean I could put something away instead of watching the account hit zero before payday. I'd like to have one month's rent saved, just one, so a bad week doesn't become a crisis. That's not a big dream, but it's mine.

say: I'd say the **robot scare** was hype and the grill still needs a human nose.
I'd joke with the line that AI only ended up writing the **menu blurb**.
think: Nothing changes for me, so my **low pay** and rising rent stay exactly where they were.
With **less than a month** saved, AI hype was never my biggest problem.
do: Keep running the **grill** and training the new commis through the winter.
Press the owner again for the **pay rise** he keeps putting off until after Christmas.
Talk the line into joining the **hospitality union** so nobody asks alone.
feel: I feel **relieved** my job is safe but **tired** of watching the account hit zero.
S0.quote: One broken tooth or a burn that keeps me off work for two weeks and we're behind on rent.
fieldNote: Her real risk is **injury without sick pay**, not technology, and she knows it.
She frames every answer around **collective bargaining**, not personal ambition.
A four-day burn last winter left the couple eating pasta for a **fortnight**.

steps.text: Keep running the Saturday grill and training the new commis
Sign the grill team up to the hospitality union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people who should worry first, and I'd mean it kindly. My cousin does bookings at a hotel and she'd be the one hit. On the line I'd say a robot can't handle a Saturday when three tables send back steaks and the fryer breaks at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the owner would use it to cut the people around me. The ordering, the rota and the bookings would go to software, the manager who does that might go, and then guess who gets the extra jobs for the same pay. Me. And slowly, the robots that flip burgers in the big chains would creep towards places like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and refuse to touch the new ordering app unless they train me on paid time. I'd get the union rep in to talk to the whole staff before any changes, not after. And I'd start picking up the odd Sunday shift at the care home kitchen up the road, just to have a second door open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit angry, because I can see how it goes. The big chains get the robots first, they drop their prices, and small places like the Copper Pot have to squeeze us to keep up. I don't hate the machines, I hate who decides how they're used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the app unless you're trained on paid time. Why draw the line there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because last time they brought in a new till, we had to learn it on our break, and it crashed every Friday for a month. If the owner wants a computer to do the ordering, he can pay for the hours it takes us to fix its mistakes. I'm not doing free work so he can save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the line would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, our nineteen-year-old on the fryer and the dish station. That's exactly the kind of work a robot arm does first, dropping baskets and loading the washer. He's a good kid and he sends half his wage home to his mum.

say: I'd say **office workers** like my cousin in hotel bookings get hit first.
I'd tell the line a robot can't handle a **Saturday rush** with the fryer down.
think: The owner would cut the people around me and hand me **extra jobs** for the same pay.
Burger **robots** in the big chains would slowly creep into places like ours.
do: Refuse the new **ordering app** unless the training happens on paid time.
Bring the **union rep** in to talk to all staff before any change.
Pick up Sunday shifts at the **care home** kitchen as a backup.
feel: I feel **uneasy** and **angry** at who gets to decide how machines are used.
S1.quote: I don't hate the machines, I hate who decides how they're used.
fieldNote: Her anger is aimed at **owners and chains**, not the technology itself.
She worries most for **Jonah**, the teenage fryer cook who supports his mother.
A buggy till learned on unpaid breaks shapes her **distrust** of new systems.

steps.text: Demand paid training time before using the new ordering app
Invite the union rep to a whole-staff meeting
Work Sunday shifts at the care home kitchen up the road

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws now, today, not after. If one company can replace every cook in the country by 2031, the government should be making them pay for it. I'd share every petition going, and I'd say it loudly at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd lose my job, maybe not in 2028, but around 2031 when the robots come. The thinking stuff, the ordering, the costing, the rota, that's not my part anyway, so for the first years I'd just watch the office side empty out. Then the robots come for the grill, and I've got nothing else. I left school for a kitchen at sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union the same month and push everyone else to. I'd stop the little extras, the takeaway coffee, the gym I never go to, to get even a few hundred saved before 2031. I wouldn't go and learn computers, I'd be bad at it and it would be gone too. I'd fight for a deal for cooks, like a payout or a guaranteed wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor going soft under me. Three years sounds like a lot until you count it in rent payments. I'd lie awake next to Tomas doing sums, and his bus job would be in the same boat, so it's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your partner's bus job would be in the same boat. What happens at home then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If both of us lose work in the same couple of years, we can't keep the flat. We'd probably move in with my mum, who has a box room and a sofa bed, and that's at twenty-seven with my partner. I'd hate it, but at least she wouldn't charge us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The warning here is only 2 years. What does that short time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no time to save anything real on my wage. With ten years I could maybe build something, but with two you just brace. The only thing that moves fast enough is people joining together and shouting.

say: I'd say we need **laws now**, before one company can replace every cook.
I'd share every **petition** and argue it loudly on the line.
think: The office side empties first, then around **2031** the robots come for my grill.
I left school for a kitchen at sixteen, so I have **no fallback** trade.
do: Join the **union** within the month and push the whole line to sign up.
Cut the coffee and the unused gym to save **a few hundred** before 2031.
Campaign for a **guaranteed wage** or payout for cooks rather than retrain.
feel: I feel like the **floor** is going soft, doing sums awake next to Tomas.
S2.quote: Three years sounds like a lot until you count it in rent payments.
fieldNote: She sees the three-year robot gap as **rent payments**, not breathing room.
Both incomes are exposed because her partner Tomas **drives buses**.
She rejects **retraining** outright, believing any new skill would vanish too.
Her fallback is her **mum's box room**, which she would hate.

steps.text: Join the hospitality union this month and recruit the line
Cancel the gym and takeaway coffees to save a few hundred
Sign and share petitions for a guaranteed wage for cooks
Move into her mum's box room if both jobs go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say we need rules, but I'd say it calmer, because there's time to win them. Five years is long enough to get a law through if people push. I'd tell friends to join something now, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've probably got until about 2034 at the grill, so seven years. I'd be thirty-four, which still feels young enough to start over, and that scares me more than it should. The thinking part goes in 2031 and I'd barely notice, the owner does the ordering anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union, help organise the other two kitchens in town, and keep cooking. I'd try to save fifty a month, which is what we can do if we stop eating out on our day off. I still wouldn't go learn AI tools, but I might do a food hygiene trainer course so I could teach in the college kitchen, because people will still teach people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It's a slow train I can see coming down the track, and at least I can step off the rails in time. The bit that scares me is how quiet everyone would be about it until it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you still wouldn't learn AI tools, but you'd consider teaching. Isn't teaching also something AI could do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the reading part, sure. But you can't learn to feel when a steak is medium rare from a screen, you learn it with someone pressing your finger into the meat. I'd bet on that lasting longer than the robots on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the nineteen-year-old on your fryer in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonah to get a proper trade now, plumbing or electrics, something with a licence. He has five years, which is more than I had at his age. I'd mean it, even if it means losing my best fryer.

say: I'd say we need **rules on robots**, and that five years is enough to win them.
I'd tell friends to **join something** now instead of waiting.
think: I've probably got until about **2034** at the grill, when I'd be thirty-four.
The **thinking side** going in 2031 barely touches me, since the owner orders anyway.
do: Help organise the **other two kitchens** in town into the union.
Save **fifty a month** by giving up eating out on the day off.
Take a **hygiene trainer** course to teach in the college kitchen.
feel: I feel **worried** but able to **breathe**, like watching a slow train coming.
S3.quote: You can't learn to feel when a steak is medium rare from a screen, you learn it with someone pressing your finger into the meat.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from **bracing** into **organising** other kitchens.
She still refuses AI tools but accepts **teaching**, which she sees as hands-on.
She would push the teenage fryer cook towards a **licensed trade**.

steps.text: Organise the two other town kitchens into the union
Save fifty a month by skipping meals out on the day off
Take a food hygiene trainer course for the college kitchen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be stupid to waste it. Governments would have time to set up proper retraining money and a basic income, so I'd vote for whoever promised that. I'd keep saying it at work until people got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a decade feels so far away that I'd probably do too little. In 2036 I'm thirty-seven, and the robots arrive about 2039, so I'd have twelve more years on the line. My knees might give out before the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking, keep my union card, and vote for the party with the best plan for workers. I'd put a little away each month, even twenty, because the habit matters more than the amount. Maybe in year five or six I'd think about the college teaching job, but I wouldn't jump early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm, because I know myself and I put things off. The money worry doesn't go anywhere just because the robots are far away. I still check the bank app before I buy a sandwich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably do too little. What would get you to move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it with my own eyes, a robot cooking in a kitchen like ours, not a video from some tech show. If the chain steakhouse on the ring road put one in, I'd be at the college the next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do with ten years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay people to retrain at full wage, not a grant that covers the bus fare. Make the companies that save money on robots pay into a fund for workers. And let unions into every kitchen, because owners won't share the savings out of kindness.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** we'd be stupid to waste.
I'd vote for whoever promises **retraining money** and a basic income.
think: Robots arrive around **2039**, giving me about twelve more years on the line.
I know I **put things off**, so I'd probably do too little.
do: Keep cooking, keep the **union card** and vote for the best plan for workers.
Save even **twenty a month** to build the habit.
Consider the **college teaching** job around year five or six.
feel: I feel **calmer** but not calm, because the **money worry** stays.
S4.quote: My knees might give out before the robots do.
fieldNote: She admits that distance breeds **delay**, and only a local robot would move her.
The long warning shifts her energy to **voting** and policy demands.
Her own body, especially her **knees**, feels like the nearer deadline.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday grill shifts and the union card
Vote for the party promising full-wage retraining
Set up a twenty-a-month standing order into savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because it hits me and Tomas at the same time with nothing saved. What would help is a law that companies replacing workers have to keep paying them for a year, and a union in every kitchen. I don't need a course in prompt writing, I need a wage while I figure it out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the owners. Everyone talks about what robots do to us, nobody asks who gets the money they save. In my kitchen the answer would be one man with a boat.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about what robots do to us, nobody asks who gets the money they save.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old grill lead** at the Copper Pot, a busy brasserie, on low pay.
She has **under a month** saved, and her partner Tomas drives buses at night.
She refuses AI tools and pins her hopes on **unions** and laws, not retraining.
Her mood stays **anxious** in most pictures and turns **alarmed** when AGI comes in 2 years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because it would hit her and Tomas together with **nothing saved**.
whatWouldHelp: A law making firms that replace workers **pay them a year**.
A **union in every kitchen** and a wage while she figures things out.
